source: Dean & Boddy (1988) An analysis of time-dependent planning
finding: Coined 'anytime algorithm'. Time-dependent planning: the time before an event varies, so a decision procedure should return a best-so-far answer whose utility is a function of computation time.
numbers: Worked example: robot classifying objects on a conveyor behind a partition. A formal framework, no experiment. Six pages (AAAI-88, pp 49-54).
quote: Anytime algorithms can be interrupted at any point during computation to return a result whose utility is a function of computation time.
limits: Formal analysis only; no empirical data. Assumes one deliberation processor, negligible preemption cost, independent events, utility monotone in time.
agent_relevance: G6: the founding case for 'always hold a best-so-far answer'. The scaffold's never-abstain rule is an anytime property.

source: Dean & Boddy (1988) five classes of performance profile
finding: Defines five capability classes: monotonic improvement; one-shot improvement (nothing until time tau, then a fixed value); linear improvement; piecewise linear with bounded utility; diminishing returns (concave, slope non-increasing).
numbers: Optimal deliberation scheduling: one-shot class is pseudo-polynomial (cites Graham 1977); linear class: always work on the event with the largest slope; diminishing-returns class has a polynomial time-slicing greedy algorithm (work on the event with the largest marginal gain at each slice, optimal within epsilon).
limits: Greedy marginal-gain rule is optimal only for concave profiles. Authors say one-shot procedures perform poorly when the time available varies.
agent_relevance: G12 and budgeting: spend each next token where the marginal quality gain is highest. An all-or-nothing pipeline is the worst profile class under uncertain time.

source: Dean & Boddy (1988) assumptions and relaxations
finding: Lists 8 assumptions (prediction time factored out, events occur on time, separate procedures per event, free preemption, cost = summed utilities, diminishing-returns procedures exist, utility monotone in time, reaction time negligible). Relaxing negligible reaction time makes the problem 'arbitrarily complex'. Utility can fall with delay when the world changes and old observations go stale.
numbers: Special case: if cost = reaction time + deliberation time, stop deliberating when the marginal gain falls to the cost slope. Assumption 5 (responses independent) is called hard to relax.
limits: Companion paper on interdependent responses was only 'in preparation'. No data.
agent_relevance: Stale-input boundary: more thinking can lower value if inputs age. Relevant to long agent loops over changing state.

source: Zilberstein (1996) Using anytime algorithms in intelligent systems, AI Magazine 17(3)
finding: Survey and framework. Seven desired properties of an anytime algorithm: measurable quality, recognizable quality, monotonicity, consistency, diminishing returns, interruptibility, preemptability. Quality metrics: certainty, accuracy, specificity.
numbers: Worked example: randomized tour improvement on 50-city TSP; quality = fraction of tour-length reduction versus the initial tour. Quality map from many runs; expected performance profile by curve fitting. Boddy and Dean used Q(t)=1-e^(-t) for an anytime planner.
quote: when quality is recognizable, the anytime algorithm can guarantee monotonicity by simply returning the best result generated so far
limits: Profiles are empirical averages over instances; one example domain, no hypothesis test. Monotonicity is guaranteed only if quality is recognizable (keep best so far).
agent_relevance: G6 and G3: keeping the best result so far when quality is recognizable is the exact rule behind submitting the best attempt. Recognizable quality needs a check the answer was not fitted to.

source: Zilberstein (1996) performance profile definitions
finding: Defines PP Q(t) (expected quality at run time t), conditional PP Pr(q_out | q_in, t), and dynamic PP Pr(q_j | q_i, t) modelled as a Markov process on the current result quality (Hansen and Zilberstein 1996).
numbers: Dynamic PP predicts improvement better when current quality is taken into account. Probability table size is a parameter trading profile accuracy for cost.
limits: Profiles must be learned from many instances; distribution shift between profiling and use breaks the prediction.
agent_relevance: Log (tokens spent, quality of current best) across items to build the agent's own profile, then set budgets from it instead of guessing.

source: Zilberstein (1996) interruptible versus contract algorithms
finding: Contract algorithms need the time allocation known in advance and may return nothing if interrupted early. Interruptible ones can be stopped any time. A general construction turns a contract algorithm into an interruptible one with a small constant penalty (Russell and Zilberstein 1991).
numbers: Penalty is a factor of 4 in time (see a07). Contract algorithms are easier to build and monitor and are the right end product when utility is predictable.
limits: Conversion cost is a worst-case bound; typical cost is lower.
agent_relevance: Maps onto LLM budgets: a fixed max_tokens run is a contract; a stop-anytime loop with a banked answer is interruptible. A reasoning model that loses its answer when truncated is a contract algorithm.

source: Zilberstein & Russell (1996) Optimal composition of real-time systems, Artificial Intelligence 82: reduction theorem
finding: Theorem 2.7 (Reduction): for any contract algorithm A an interruptible algorithm B can be built with q_B(4t) >= q_A(t), by running A repeatedly with exponentially increasing time limits.
numbers: Time factor 4: if interrupted at t, the last finished contract has length at least t/4. Doubling schedule 1, 2, 4, 8. For search this yields iterative deepening automatically.
quote: Construct B by running A repeatedly with exponentially increasing time limits.
limits: Worst-case constant for a single contract algorithm; wastes up to about 75 percent of time at the moment of interruption.
agent_relevance: Gives a doubling schedule for the agent: attempt with budget b, then 2b, 4b, keeping the best passing answer. Waste is bounded by constant 4 against knowing the deadline.

source: Zilberstein & Russell (1996) composition and compilation complexity
finding: Allocating time among anytime modules to maximise system quality is NP-complete in the strong sense (reduction from partially ordered knapsack). Local compilation on tree-structured, bounded-degree programs is linear and globally optimal if each module is input-monotone (deterministic profiles) or input-linear (probabilistic profiles).
numbers: Theorem 1: NP-complete in the strong sense. Theorem 2: local compilation optimal under input monotonicity. Theorem 3: probabilistic case needs input linearity, called 'not very realistic'; piecewise-linear approximation suggested.
limits: Tree-structured assumption fails when sub-results are shared, e.g. F=E(D(B(A(x)),C(A(x)))). Only approximate methods then.
agent_relevance: The staged scaffold (S0-S9): splitting time across stages is itself a hard problem. Simple fixed shares or greedy marginal gain are the realistic options; do not expect optimal splits.

source: Zilberstein (1996) run-time monitoring and optimal stopping conditions
finding: Three monitoring strategies: fixed contract (optimal when utility is predictable and the profile deterministic, Theorem 4), marginal value of computation (myopic: stop when the expected gain of one more step is negative), and monitoring policies that price the monitoring itself.
numbers: Theorem 5: myopic value-of-computation stopping is optimal when the profile is monotone increasing and concave-down AND the cost of time is monotone increasing and concave-up.
limits: A profile with plateaus or later jumps (non-concave) makes myopic stopping quit too early. Monitoring cost ignored by the myopic rule.
agent_relevance: G1/G6/G12: stop only on a real signal that the marginal gain is gone, and remember the sufficient condition: reasoning with sudden jumps is not concave.

source: Zilberstein (1996) applications and open questions
finding: Applications: Bayesian network evaluation, model-based diagnosis, database query processing, constraint satisfaction, sensor interpretation, path planning. Open monitoring questions: how much performance variance justifies run-time monitoring, how often to monitor, how coarse a quality estimate is tolerable.
numbers: No benchmark numbers; survey citing Horvitz (1987, 1990), Russell and Wefald (1989, 1991), Liu et al. (1991) imprecise computation, Garvey and Lesser design-to-time.
limits: Review, not an experiment. No human-subject data.
agent_relevance: Pointers for sibling subfields: flexible computation and value of computation (metareasoning subfield).

source: Simon (1955) A behavioral model of rational choice, QJE 69; Simon (1956) Rational choice and the structure of the environment
finding: Founding statement of bounded rationality and satisficing: agents search until an aspiration level is met rather than optimise. NOT opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota exhausted); stated from general knowledge only.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified here. Aspiration adjustment over time is the link to quality-as-a-function-of-time. Covered by the sibling subfield on bounded rationality and satisficing.
agent_relevance: Satisficing is the human ancestor of the anytime stop rule: stop when good enough. Re-read the primary text before quoting.

source: Russell & Wefald (1991) Do the right thing; Horvitz (1987, 1990) flexible computation; Boddy & Dean (1994) deliberation scheduling
finding: Value of computation (Russell and Wefald) and flexible computation (Horvitz) treat each reasoning step as an action with expected utility gain against time cost. Not opened; known here only through the opened Zilberstein review.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Second-hand. Details belong to the metareasoning subfield (C12/05).
agent_relevance: Same stop rule as Theorem 5 seen from the metareasoning side.

source: Hansen & Zilberstein (2001) Monitoring and control of anytime algorithms: a dynamic programming approach, AIJ 126
finding: Treats stop-or-continue as a sequential decision problem solved by dynamic programming over a Markov dynamic profile, giving a non-myopic stopping policy. Only an abstract-level summary seen through search; no PDF opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract level only. Extends the myopic rule of Theorem 5, which fails on non-concave profiles.
agent_relevance: Candidate method for a stop rule when profiles have plateaus. Read in full before use.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Test-time compute efficacy depends on question difficulty. Beam search is better on harder questions and at low budgets; best-of-N is better on easier questions and at high budgets. A compute-optimal policy that picks the method by predicted difficulty beats fixed methods.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute (e.g. 16 vs 64 generations). FLOPs-matched comparison against a 14x larger pretrained model: test-time compute is often preferable on easy and intermediate questions, and sometimes on hard ones; pretraining is better on the hardest.
limits: PaLM 2 models on MATH only. Difficulty must be predicted (oracle bins give larger gains than predicted bins). Verifier can be exploited: beam search on easy questions amplifies verifier artifacts and degrades results.
agent_relevance: G12: per-item budget should depend on difficulty, and heavy search on easy items can hurt. Supports a cheap difficulty probe before spending tokens.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction of problems solved by any of k samples) grows log-linearly with k and fits an exponentiated power law over orders of magnitude, so the quality-versus-compute curve for verifiable tasks keeps rising.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% solved with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples, against the then single-sample state of the art of 43%.
limits: Needs an automatic verifier; without one, picking the right sample is the bottleneck. Coverage is not accuracy. Samples from one model are correlated.
agent_relevance: Agrees with G3/G4: repeated attempts pay only with a real check; agreement is not proof. The anytime curve on verifiable items is long-tailed, not flat.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing is an anytime control for an LLM: cut thinking by appending an end-of-thinking delimiter (interrupt), or lengthen it by suppressing the delimiter and appending 'Wait'. With 1,000 SFT samples (s1K) on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, accuracy rises with thinking tokens.
numbers: AIME24: 50.0% without budget forcing, 56.7% with it (s1-32B). Forcing 2, 4 or 6 'Wait' continuations extrapolated AIME24 from 50% to 57%. Table 3 (AIME24, 5 runs for most rows): budget forcing Control 100%, Scaling slope 15, Performance 56.7; token-conditional prompting Control 40%, slope -24, Perf 40.0; step-conditional Control 60%, Perf 36.7; rejection sampling Control 100%, slope -35, Perf 40.0.
quote: we suppress the generation of the end-of-thinking token delimiter and optionally append the string 'Wait'
limits: Flattens after a few forced continuations and is capped by the context window: with up to 512 steps, 12 of 30 AIME24 questions exceeded the context and accuracy dropped. Model cannot reliably count tokens even when trained to. 30-question benchmark is noisy.
agent_relevance: Measured anytime curve for an LLM and a working interrupt mechanism. Supports G6: on forced stop, answer from the partial trace. 'Wait' is a forced doubt, so it is in tension with G1 and works only on a trained model with a ceiling.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Optimizing anytime reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization (AnytimeReasoner), NeurIPS 2025
finding: RL objective for anytime LLM reasoning: sample a thinking budget from a prior over {b1..bm}, truncate the thought there, force a summary answer, and reward each budget. With a uniform prior the objective is the area under the score-versus-budget curve. Thinking and summary policies are optimised separately; BRPO reduces variance using earlier budget rewards. Cites Dean and Boddy 1988 and Zilberstein and Russell 1995 as source of the idea.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B trained one epoch on 40,315 DeepScaleR problems, 8 A100, under 10% extra cost vs GRPO. Final accuracy at 8000 tokens, average of 5 benchmarks: base 39.8, GRPO 43.0, AnytimeReasoner-base 44.9. AIME24: 16.3 base, 19.0 GRPO, 21.9 AR-base, 22.9 AR-uniform. Evaluated at 32 budgets 250 tokens apart; training uses at most 8 budgets. Reports 32.7% vs a prior 30.3% on AIME24 in a comparable setting.
quote: Anytime algorithms ... can be interrupted at any point during computation, providing the best possible solution so far
limits: 1.5B distilled model, math only; no seed variance seen in the text read. Part of the gain comes from the decoupled summary and variance reduction rather than budget sampling: AR-base (no budget sampling) already beats GRPO.
agent_relevance: Quality-as-a-function-of-time can be trained for, and a forced summary at a cutoff gives a usable answer. For a no-training agent the summary-at-cutoff step is what can be copied.

source: Aggarwal & Welleck (2025) L1: controlling how long a reasoning model thinks with reinforcement learning, COLM 2025
finding: Length Controlled Policy Optimization (LCPO) trains a 1.5B reasoning model (from DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview) to meet a prompted token target, exactly (L1-Exact) or as a maximum (L1-Max). Gives a smooth controllable accuracy-versus-tokens curve with log-linear scaling.
numbers: Versus S1 budget forcing: over 100% relative and 20-25% absolute accuracy gain at 512 and 1024 token budgets on math. Log-linear slope 0.24 for L1 vs 0.37 for S1. L1-Exact about 1% below DeepScaleR-4K (same base, no length control). Training 700 steps, 4K context in training, 8K at eval.
limits: Small 1.5B model; the large relative gain comes from weak S1 numbers at tiny budgets. The caller picks the target, so stopping is not adaptive per item.
agent_relevance: A model can be taught a budget dial. Not usable by a scaffold without training; useful contrast: S1 has the steeper slope but weak low-budget quality.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic early exit in reasoning models (DEER)
finding: Training-free adaptive stopping: at thought-switch points, prompt the model to emit a trial answer and read its confidence; exit when confidence passes a threshold. Value-of-computation stopping built from the model's own confidence.
numbers: Across 11 reasoning models and 10 benchmarks, CoT length cut by an average of 19.1% to 80.1% while accuracy improved by 0.3% to 5.0%. Latency down 27.9% for original DEER; branch-parallel variant down 36.3% to 58.6%. Threshold too low gives sharp accuracy drops; too high exits late.
limits: Trial-answer overhead hurts code tasks where trial answers are long. Confidence is the model's own, so G5/G8 caution: self-grading is a weak signal; threshold needs per-model tuning.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue of an anytime stop rule. Test our stop trigger with agreement among independent trial answers or a code check instead of self-reported confidence.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend far more compute than needed on easy questions; later solutions in a long trace add little. In correct traces the first correct answer usually appears early, so later rounds are redundant.
numbers: For 'what is 2 plus 3?' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. Their self-training simplification cut token output by 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview while keeping accuracy.
limits: A few open o1-like models in 2024; easy-question focus; the fix needs fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Evidence for G12: diminishing returns are steep on easy items; stop-on-first-verified-answer would save most tokens.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute, TMLR
finding: Constructed tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraint tracking, advanced-AI-risk probes. This violates the monotonicity property of anytime theory.
numbers: Claude Opus 4 accuracy falls from nearly 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning extends on distractor tasks; in the natural-overthinking setup DeepSeek R1 falls from 70% to 30% with five distractors.
limits: Tasks were built adversarially, so they bound the failure rather than estimate its prevalence. Patterns differ by model.
agent_relevance: Boundary for G1/G6: quality can fall with time, so 'best so far' must be picked by a check, not by taking the latest answer.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does thinking more always help? Mirage of test-time scaling in reasoning models
finding: Accuracy rises with thinking then falls (non-monotone). The early rise is attributed to higher output variance, via a simple probabilistic model. They propose parallel thinking: several independent paths in the same budget with majority vote.
numbers: Parallel thinking gives up to 20% higher accuracy than extended thinking; at a 16K token budget up to 22% higher than sequential scaling.
limits: Majority vote assumes independent errors, which G4 says one model violates; gain may be smaller on correlated tasks. Mechanism is a model, not an internal ablation.
agent_relevance: Argues against a single long trace: splitting a budget over independent tries can beat it. Tension with the interruptible view; test on our items.

source: Synthesis (opened sources): concavity and monotonicity do not hold cleanly for LLM reasoning curves
finding: LLM quality curves are only roughly concave. s1 shows a rise, a plateau, then a context-limited drop; the inverse-scaling tasks show a fall; Mirage shows a rise then a fall. Zilberstein Theorem 5 (myopic stopping optimal) needs a concave profile and convex time cost, so it is not guaranteed.
numbers: Evidence: s1 12 of 30 AIME24 questions exceeded context at 512 steps; DeepSeek R1 70% to 30% with five distractors; Claude Opus 4 about 100% to 85-90%.
limits: Our own synthesis of opened sources, not a measured test of concavity.
agent_relevance: Design: do not rely on one marginal-gain stop rule. Add an external check (G3) and a hard cap, and test the stop rule on a held-out set of our own items.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1 Table 1 comparison with other 32B reasoning models
finding: With only 1,000 training examples plus budget forcing, s1-32B is competitive with models trained on far more data, and budget forcing alone adds several points on AIME24 and GPQA.
numbers: Columns AIME24 / MATH500 / GPQA: s1-32B 56.7 / 93.0 / 59.6; s1 without budget forcing 50.0 / 92.6 / 56.6; Bespoke-32B (17K examples) 63.3 / 93.0 / 58.1; Sky-T1 (17K) 43.3 / 82.4 / 56.8; o1-preview 44.6 / 85.5 / 73.3.
limits: Single run per cell in the main table; AIME24 has 30 questions so one question is 3.3 points. s1 later released a s1.1 variant that scores higher.
agent_relevance: Budget forcing gains (+6.7 AIME24, +3.0 GPQA) are small next to the noise of a 30-item test; our own tests need more items.

source: Qi et al. (2025) AnytimeReasoner effect of the budget prior
finding: Three priors compared when training the thinking policy: base (only the max budget), uniform, and linear (probability proportional to budget). All beat GRPO at every budget. Uniform wins at small budgets; at large budgets all priors converge to similar accuracy.
numbers: Evaluated at 32 budgets from 0 to 8000 tokens; 320 sampled thinking processes per AIME/AMC question and 80 per other question. AIME24 final accuracy 21.9 (base), 22.3 (linear), 22.9 (uniform) against GRPO 19.0.
limits: Same 1.5B model and math-only setting; differences between priors at large budgets are small and no confidence intervals were seen.
agent_relevance: The area-under-curve objective helps most where budgets are tight, which is the regime a cost-limited agent lives in.
